title: Because Exodus 31 hides a shock most believers miss.
paragraphs: Because Exodus 31 hides a shock most believers miss.
When God announced the building of the Tabernacle—the most sacred structure Israel would ever see—you might expect Him to choose a prophet, a priest, or a famous spiritual leader.
But He didn’t.
God chose a craftsman.

A man with tools in his hands.
Dust on his skin.
Calluses on his fingers.
His name was Bezalel.
And the Lord said something that should shake every believer awake:
“See, I have called by name Bezalel… and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship.” — Exodus 31:2–3
Pause there.
The first person in the Bible explicitly described as being filled with the Spirit of God was not introduced as a preacher, king, or miracle worker.

He was an artist.
A builder.
A craftsman.
Let that sink in.
Because many people believe a dangerous lie:
That God only values what happens on a stage.
But Exodus 31 destroys that idea.
God anoints hands.
Hands that design.
Hands that sew.
Hands that carve wood.
Hands that melt gold.
Hands that work quietly while others stand in the spotlight.
Bezalel was chosen to help build the Tabernacle, the sacred tent where God's presence would dwell among Israel. Every measurement, every woven thread, every hammered piece of gold mattered.
Why?
Because the Tabernacle wasn’t just architecture.
It was theology in wood, gold, and fabric.

The Ark.
The lampstand.
The altar.
The veil.
Every detail preached a message:

God is holy.
Sin is serious.
And sinners cannot approach Him casually.
Yet God made a way.
But here’s the deeper layer most people miss.
The Tabernacle was never meant to be the final answer.
It was a shadow.
A prophetic picture pointing forward to someone greater.
Jesus Christ.
The Gospel of John reveals the connection when it says:
“The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” — John 1:14
That word dwelt literally means “tabernacled.”
Jesus became the true meeting place between God and humanity.
Where the Tabernacle had curtains, Christ tore the veil.
Where priests offered sacrifices daily, Jesus offered Himself once for all (Hebrews 10:10–12).
Where the Ark symbolized God's throne, Christ now sits at the right hand of the Father as our living High Priest.
The Tabernacle was the shadow.
Jesus is the reality.
But there’s something else in this story that cuts straight into the heart.
Many people want the platform.
But God often calls people to the workbench.
We crave recognition.
God often assigns faithfulness.
We want applause.
God looks for obedience.
Bezalel was not building his own brand.
He was building something for God’s glory.
And here’s the astonishing truth:
The Spirit of God empowered him not just for worship—but for craftsmanship.
Meaning this:
Your skill can be sacred.
Your work can be worship.
Your profession can become a platform for God's glory.
The Spirit who filled Bezalel is the same Spirit who empowers believers today.

Whether you design…
Build…
Write…
Code…
Teach…
Repair…
Lead…
Create…
When your life belongs to Christ, everything becomes holy ground.
But let’s be honest.
Many of us have used our talents for the wrong things.
Hands meant for worship have been used for sin.
Minds designed for creativity have been consumed by pride.
Skills given by God have been twisted for self-glory.
That’s the scandal of the human heart.
But here’s the miracle of the Gospel:
Jesus doesn’t just forgive sinners.
He redeems them.
He restores what sin tried to destroy.
He takes broken lives and rebuilds them into something beautiful.
Just like Bezalel shaped gold for the Tabernacle, Christ shapes redeemed sinners into living stones for His kingdom.
The apostle Peter writes:
God is still building.
But now the structure is not made of curtains and wood.
It’s made of redeemed people.
Men and women saved by grace.
Former rebels turned into worshipers.
Former sinners turned into testimonies.
And here’s the invitation.
Stop chasing recognition.
Start pursuing obedience.
Stop measuring your life by visibility.
Start measuring it by faithfulness.
Because the same God who called Bezalel by name still calls people today.
He calls the unseen.
The overlooked.
The ordinary.
And He fills them with His Spirit to build something that lasts beyond this life.
So here’s the question:
Are you using what God gave you for His glory?
Or are you still building your own kingdom?
Because one day, every work will be tested by fire (1 Corinthians 3:13).
Only what was built for Christ will remain.
But here is the hope that changes everything.
Even if your past is filled with failure…
Even if your hands have built the wrong things…
Jesus can still redeem your story.
Repent.
Turn to Christ.
Trust the One who died for sinners and rose again.
And let Him take your life—your gifts, your skills, your story—and use them for His glory.
Because the greatest Builder in the universe is still at work.
And He is not just building a tabernacle.
He is building His Kingdom.
And the invitation is open.
Follow Jesus.
Surrender your life.
And become part of the masterpiece God is crafting through grace.
Because the world celebrates fame…
But heaven celebrates faithfulness.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
